t1.text: The anatomy of an L L M. What you are actually buying, in under three minutes.

c1.text: When you send a message, the model never sees just your question.

c2.text: The system prompt, the whole conversation, retrieved documents and tool outputs are stitched into one long context. And all of it is billed.

k1.text: A tokenizer chops that text into sub-word pieces called tokens, and each one becomes a number.

k2.text: "The cat sat on the" is five tokens. Tokens are the unit on your invoice.

e1.text: Each number then looks up a vector of thousands of values. Meaning, encoded as geometry.

l1.text: Those vectors flow through a stack of about eighty identical transformer layers.

l2.text: Inside every layer, attention lets each token look back at the ones before it. The last "the" pulls hardest on "sat" and "cat".

p1.text: At the top of the stack, the model scores every one of a hundred thousand possible next tokens. "Mat" wins, and a sampler picks it.

p2.text: Then that token is fed straight back in, and the whole stack runs again. One full pass, for every word you see streaming onto your screen.

f1.text: That loop splits every request into two phases.

f2.text: Prefill reads your entire prompt in one parallel pass. Fast, and cheap.

f3.text: Decode writes the answer one token at a time, and every token re-reads all of the model's weights from memory.

f4.text: That is why output tokens cost three to eight times more than input.

f5.text: The same physics makes the discounts honest. Cached prompts skip re-reading, for about ninety percent off. Batch lanes run at half price.

d0.text: Finally, five hidden dials quietly change your bill. Two are set by the model maker, two by whoever serves the model, and one is yours.

d1.text: One. The tokenizer. The same sentence costs almost seven times more tokens in Hindi than in English.

d2.text: Two. Architecture. A trillion-parameter mixture of experts wakes up only about thirty-seven billion per token, so it can be cheaper than a dense seventy-billion model.

d3.text: Three. Precision. Going from sixteen bits to eight, to four, halves the memory read per token, each step.

d4.text: Four. Batching. Thirty-two requests share one read of the weights, cutting cost per token by over ninety percent. The biggest lever of all.

d5.text: And five. The context you send. Your system prompt is re-sent, and re-billed, on every single turn.

o1.text: Sequential generation. Memory. Weight reads. That is the machine behind every price in this guide.

o2.text: Now open each chapter, and try the dials yourself.
